title: At least one boy: both boys?
hook: Two children, and at least one is a boy. Surely the other is 50/50?

knows: each child is a boy or a girl with chance about 1/2, independently
doesNotKnow: how a piece of information narrows the set of possible cases
that differently worded clues remove different cases

misconception: Knowing one child is a boy leaves the other as 50/50, so both being boys has chance 1/2.
objective: The learner can explain that 'at least one is a boy' removes only the girl-girl family, leaving three equally likely families of which one is boy-boy (1/3), while 'the older is a boy' removes two and gives 1/2.

claims.text: Two-child families come in four equally likely kinds by older and younger child: boy-boy, boy-girl, girl-boy, girl-girl.
claims.source: Model assumption: each child independently a boy or girl with chance 1/2 (real birth ratios are about 105 boys to 100 girls, which shifts the answers only slightly).

claims.text: If you learn only that at least one child is a boy, the chance both are boys is 1/3.
claims.source: Enumeration: the clue removes GG, leaving BB, BG, GB; 1 of 3 (exact() in src/demos/probability/at-least-one-boy/model.ts).

claims.text: If you learn that the older child is a boy, the chance both are boys is 1/2.
claims.source: Enumeration: the clue leaves BB, BG; 1 of 2.

claims.text: The answer depends on how the information was obtained; the lesson uses the rule that you learn only the clue itself.
claims.source: M. Gardner (1959), Mathematical Games, Scientific American, May and October 1959; see also Bar-Hillel & Falk (1982), Cognition 11: 109-122.

claims.text: Of the stage's 1,000 families, 744 have at least one boy and 240 of those are boy-boy (32%); 504 have an older boy and 240 of those are boy-boy (48%).
claims.source: families() in model.ts, seed 1959, untuned (the first seed tried). Over seeds 1-500 the at-least-one share had middle 95% 29.9%-36.7% (median 33.3%) and the older-boy share 45.9%-54.6% (median 50.1%).

recall.question: You learn only that a two-child family has at least one girl. What is the chance both children are girls?
recall.why: The clue removes only boy-boy. Girl-girl, girl-boy and boy-girl remain, equally likely, and one of the three is girl-girl.
